meta.title: EU AI Act – Risk Tier Self-Assessment
changelog: 1.2.0 – Plain-language rewrite of every question, explainer and answer. The exact wording of the law now lives in a collapsible 'In the words of the law' panel (node.legalText) and each checklist item keeps its exact legal phrasing on expand (item.label) beside a plain summary (item.plain). Added an explicit 'I'm not sure' answer on judgement-heavy questions that routes conservatively and records a review flag.
1.1.0 – Added cross-links, official guideline links + examples, FOSS exemption note, provider/deployer obligation split, optional context step.
meta.purpose: Help the owner of an algorithm or AI application find out, in plain language, which risk category of the EU AI Act their system falls into: out of scope, prohibited, high-risk (Annex I or Annex III), limited-risk (transparency) or minimal-risk. A separate overlay covers general-purpose AI (GPAI) models.
meta.disclaimer: This tool gives you a first, indicative answer. It is not legal advice and it is not binding. It is based on the AI Act and the European Commission's guidance (the high-risk classification guidance is still a draft). The final call is the provider's responsibility, checked by the market surveillance authority, and only the Court of Justice of the EU can give a binding interpretation. When in doubt, ask the AI Act Service Desk, your authority, or a lawyer.

languageStyle.note: Every screen has three layers. Show them in this priority: (1) the plain-language question + explainer (node.text, node.explainer) — always visible; (2) an 'In the words of the law' collapsible holding the exact/near-verbatim regulation wording (node.legalText) — collapsed by default; (3) an 'Examples / how to decide' collapsible holding node.help (likelyYes / likelyNo) — collapsed by default. Checklist items follow the same idea: item.plain is the visible line, item.label + item.ref are the exact wording shown on expand.
languageStyle.tone: Warm, direct, second person ('your system'). Short sentences. Avoid article numbers in the main text; keep them in the legalText panel and the small reference chips.

fossExemption.title: A note if your system is open-source
fossExemption.body: If your AI system is released under a free and open-source licence, the AI Act mostly leaves it alone. But there's an important catch: this free pass does NOT apply if the system is high-risk, banned, or one of the systems that must be transparent with people. In those three cases the rules apply even to open-source. Separately, open-source general-purpose models get a lighter documentation load, except when the model is a very powerful 'systemic-risk' one. Even then, an open-source model still needs a copyright policy and a public summary of its training data.
fossExemption.howToShow: Show as an info note on the minimal-risk and GPAI result cards, and whenever the user says the system is open-source. Never let 'open-source' downgrade a banned, high-risk or transparency result: show the note but keep the category.

providerVsDeployer.title: Who has to do what: makers vs users
providerVsDeployer.body: The duties depend on your role. A 'provider' builds the system (or model) and puts it on the market under its own name. A 'deployer' uses the system in its own work. Most of the heavy duties (building it safely, documentation, the conformity check) fall on the provider. Deployers have a shorter list: use it as instructed, keep a human in the loop, monitor it, and in some cases run a fundamental-rights impact check. Watch out: if a user rebrands a system, changes it substantially, or uses it for a new purpose that makes it high-risk, that user legally becomes a provider.
providerVsDeployer.howToShow: Use the role context flag to show the relevant obligations first, with a 'show all roles' toggle.

resultModel.description: The assessment produces a compiled PROFILE, not a single leaf: a system can carry several statuses at once. Accumulate flags and render all applicable result cards, filtered by role, with the FOSS note where relevant, and a 'worth double-checking' box listing any review flags.

dimensions.primaryTier: out_of_scope | prohibited | high_risk_annex_i | high_risk_annex_iii | not_high_risk_filtered | minimal_risk. Set by the SPINE.
dimensions.transparency: List of triggered Art. 50 items (some auto-derived). Cumulative with any tier except out_of_scope and prohibited.
dimensions.gpai: none | gpai_model | gpai_model_systemic. Independent of the system tier.
dimensions.role: provider | deployer | both | unknown. Only filters which obligations are shown.
dimensions.fossLicence: yes | no | unknown. Only surfaces the FOSS note.
dimensions.reviewFlags: Array of { node, note } collected whenever the user chose an 'I'm not sure' answer. Rendered as a 'Worth double-checking with an expert' box on the result screen. Does not change the tier.

shortCircuits: out_of_scope: stop. Do not run transparency or GPAI.
prohibited: stop the tier spine (banned overrides everything, including open-source). Still note GPAI if relevant; transparency is moot.

crossLinks.description: Links that let the tool ask fewer questions and stay consistent. The implementer MUST apply these.

rules.when: The user selects 'biometric categorisation' (1(b)) or 'emotion recognition' (1(c)) at S4.
rules.then: Automatically add the Art. 50(3) 'tell people they are exposed to it' duty. At T0, show that item pre-ticked and locked, with a 'we worked this out from your earlier answer' tag. Don't ask it again.

rules.when: Emotion recognition or biometric categorisation is in play.
rules.then: Remind the user these can be BANNED rather than high-risk: reading emotions at work or school (Art. 5(1)(f)), and sorting people by sensitive traits (Art. 5(1)(g)). Already screened at S1; show a reminder so a banned system isn't mislabelled as merely high-risk.

rules.when: The user ticks 'deep fakes' (50(4)) at T0.
rules.then: Point out that deep fakes are AI-generated content, so the 'mark it as AI-made' duty (50(2), on the provider) probably also applies. Suggest, don't force.

S0_ai_system.text: Is your system an artificial intelligence tool?
S0_ai_system.explainer: An artificial intelligence tool is a computer-based system that: can work with some degree of independence; may adapt after it has been put into use; and uses the information it receives to work out how to produce results, such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions that can affect the physical or digital world. The crucial feature is inference: the system analyses data and derives an output from it, for example through machine learning or logic-based methods. It does more than simply follow a fixed set of rules written entirely by humans.

legalText.text: 'AI system' means a machine-based system that is designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments.

likelyYes: It uses machine learning (it was trained on data)
It reasons with knowledge or logic rules to work things out, or searches for/optimises solutions
It produces content, predictions, recommendations or decisions from data, with some independence
likelyNo: It just speeds up a maths calculation or a classic method
It only follows fixed formulas or rules a person wrote (like a spreadsheet or a simple database query)
It's a simple rule-of-thumb or a single basic statistical rule, with no learning

options.label: Yes, it is an artificial intelligence tool
No, it only runs pre-written code / fixed rules
I'm not sure whether it 'infers'
options.reviewNote: Whether your system 'infers' (rather than just following fixed rules) decides if the AI Act applies at all. Check the AI-system definition guidance or ask an expert.

C0_context.explainer: This won't change your result. It just lets us show the duties that actually apply to you, and the right note if your system is open-source. Feel free to skip it.

fields.label: What's your role with this system?

options.label: I build it / put it on the market (provider)
I use it in my organisation (deployer)

fields.label: Is it released under a free and open-source licence?

S1_prohibited.text: Does your system do any of the things the AI Act bans outright?
S1_prohibited.explainer: A small number of AI uses are banned in the EU because they're considered too harmful. Have a quick look through the list. If your system does any of them, it's banned, whatever else is true. Two to watch: reading people's emotions at work or school, and sorting people by sensitive traits (like race or beliefs), are usually banned rather than just 'high-risk'.

legalText.text: Article 5 prohibits, among others: manipulative or deceptive techniques and exploitation of vulnerabilities that cause significant harm; social scoring; predicting crime based solely on profiling; untargeted scraping of facial images; emotion recognition in the workplace and education; biometric categorisation inferring sensitive attributes; and real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement (with narrow exceptions).

options.label: Yes, at least one of these applies

S2_annex_i_product.text: Is your system part of a physical product that already has EU safety rules?
S2_annex_i_product.explainer: Some products, like machines, medical devices, toys, cars or lifts, must already meet EU safety law before they can be sold. This route applies if your AI is one of those products, or is a part that keeps it safe (a 'safety component', meaning something whose failure could hurt people, or that does a safety job). Features that only improve comfort, efficiency or convenience usually don't count.

legalText.text: An AI system is high-risk under Article 6(1) where it is itself a product, or is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I. 'Safety component' (Art. 3(14)) means a component which fulfils a safety function for that product, or the failure or malfunctioning of which endangers the health and safety of persons or property.

likelyYes: Your AI is, or sits inside, a regulated product (medical device, machine, vehicle, lift, toy, radio equipment)
It does a safety job (spots a person and triggers a safe stop; prevents a collision)
If it failed, someone could get hurt (lane-keeping, lift-door control)
likelyNo: It only improves comfort, efficiency or convenience, and a failure would just be annoying or costly
The product isn't covered by any EU product-safety law

options.label: Yes, it's a regulated product or a safety part of one
I'm not sure
options.reviewNote: Whether your AI is a regulated product or a safety component can be technical. We've kept you on the product-safety route so you also see the next question; confirm with the relevant product legislation or an expert.

S3_annex_i_tpca.text: Does that product need to be checked by an independent body before it's sold?
S3_annex_i_tpca.explainer: For your AI to be high-risk on this route, an outside body (a 'notified body') has to be involved in approving the product, not just your own company. If you're allowed to sign it off yourself, this route does not make it high-risk.

legalText.text: The second cumulative condition of Article 6(1): the product whose safety component is the AI system, or the AI system itself as a product, is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to the placing on the market or putting into service of that product pursuant to the Annex I legislation.

likelyYes: The product law requires a notified body (e.g. many medical devices, higher-risk machinery)
likelyNo: You can self-certify with internal checks only

options.label: Yes, an independent body must check it
I'm not sure
options.reviewNote: If an independent ('notified') body must approve the product, your AI is high-risk on the product-safety route. Check the specific product legislation to be sure.

S4_annex_iii_area.text: Is your system used for one of the sensitive purposes on the AI Act's high-risk list?
S4_annex_iii_area.explainer: The AI Act singles out certain uses, across eight areas, as high-risk because they can seriously affect people's lives. The areas cover things like hiring and managing staff, credit and insurance, education, essential services, law enforcement, migration, and justice and elections. Only the specific uses listed under each area count, not the whole area. Tick anything that matches what your system is actually meant to do. Many only apply when the system assesses people, not just companies.

legalText.text: AI systems referred to in Annex III shall be considered high-risk. Annex III lists eight areas (biometrics; critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment and workers' management; access to essential private and public services; law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control; administration of justice and democratic processes) and, under each, an exhaustive list of specific use cases.

options.label: Yes, it matches at least one listed use
I'm not sure
options.reviewNote: If you're unsure whether your use is on the high-risk list, we've treated it as possibly high-risk so you see the rest of the checks. Compare your exact purpose against the Annex III list or ask an expert.

S5_profiling.text: Does your system build a profile of individual people?
S5_profiling.explainer: 'Profiling' means automatically analysing someone's personal data to evaluate or predict things about them, for example their performance at work, health, finances, interests, reliability, behaviour, or where they are and where they go. If your system does this, the AI Act always treats it as high-risk, and the exemptions on the next screen can't be used.

legalText.text: An AI system referred to in Annex III shall always be considered high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons. 'Profiling' (Art. 4(4) GDPR) means any form of automated processing of personal data to evaluate certain personal aspects relating to a natural person, in particular to analyse or predict aspects concerning performance at work, economic situation, health, personal preferences, interests, reliability, behaviour, location or movements.

options.label: I'm not sure
options.reviewNote: If it turns out your system profiles people, it is automatically high-risk and the exemptions don't apply. We've let you check the exemptions, but confirm the profiling question carefully.

S6_filter.text: Could your system be exempt because it only plays a limited, supporting role?
S6_filter.explainer: Even if your use is on the high-risk list, it might not count as high-risk if it only does a narrow, supporting job and doesn't really affect the final decision. You qualify only if at least one of the situations on this screen fits your system AND it doesn't meaningfully sway the outcome. These are read strictly. This escape hatch does not apply if your system profiles people, or if it's part of a bigger setup that together does affect decisions.

legalText.text: By way of derogation, an Annex III system is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, because it: (a) performs a narrow procedural task; (b) improves the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) detects decision-making patterns or deviations and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review; or (d) performs a preparatory task to a relevant assessment.

options.label: Yes, one of these fits and it doesn't drive the decision
No, none really fits (or it does affect the outcome)
I'm not sure
options.reviewNote: You can only rely on this exemption if you can clearly show and document that one of the conditions fits. If you're not sure, it's safer to treat the system as high-risk for now.

T0_transparency.text: Does your system need to be open with people in any of these ways?
T0_transparency.explainer: Some AI systems have to be upfront about what they are, whatever their risk level. These duties stack on top of your category. Tick anything that applies. Anything we already worked out from your earlier answers is ticked for you and locked. If none applies and your system isn't high-risk, it's minimal-risk.

legalText.text: Article 50 sets transparency obligations: informing people when they interact with an AI system; marking AI-generated or manipulated audio, image, video and text in a machine-readable way; informing people exposed to emotion-recognition or biometric-categorisation systems; and disclosing deep fakes and AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest.

G0_gpai.text: Did you build a general-purpose ('foundation') AI model?
G0_gpai.explainer: This is a separate question about the model itself, not how it's used. A general-purpose model is a large model, trained on huge amounts of data, that can handle many different tasks, like a large language model or a big image generator. If you only use or fine-tune someone else's model to build your app, these duties usually sit with the maker of the original model, unless you change it substantially.

legalText.text: 'General-purpose AI model' means an AI model, including where trained with a large amount of data using self-supervision at scale, that displays significant generality and is capable of competently performing a wide range of distinct tasks regardless of the way the model is placed on the market, and that can be integrated into a variety of downstream systems or applications.

likelyYes: You trained a large model that works across many tasks (a language model, a big image/audio/video model)
You put a foundation model out there for others to build on
likelyNo: Your model does one specific job only
You just call or fine-tune someone else's model without changing it much

options.label: Yes, I provide a general-purpose model
No, it's a specific-purpose system, or I use someone else's model
I'm not sure
options.reviewNote: You might be a general-purpose AI model provider, which carries its own duties. Check the 'duties for GPAI model providers' guidance to be sure.

G1_systemic.text: Is your model one of the most powerful, 'systemic-risk' models?
G1_systemic.explainer: The most capable general-purpose models carry extra duties. Yours is presumed to be in this group if training it used more than 10^25 FLOP of computing power (a very high bar that only the largest models reach today), or if the Commission has formally designated it. Most models are not in this group.

legalText.text: A general-purpose AI model has systemic risk if it has high-impact capabilities (presumed where the cumulative amount of computation used for its training exceeds 10^25 floating point operations) or is designated as such by the Commission. Such models are subject to the additional obligations in Article 55.

likelyYes: The Commission has designated your model
likelyNo: Training was well below that bar and there's no designation

options.label: Yes (over the 10^25 FLOP bar, or designated)
I'm not sure
options.reviewNote: The systemic-risk bar is very high, so most models are below it. If your training compute was anywhere near 10^25 FLOP, check the GPAI guidance, as the extra duties are significant.

RESULT.text: Show all applicable result cards from the flags (primary tier + transparency + GPAI), with obligations filtered by role, the FOSS note where relevant, and a 'worth double-checking' box listing any review flags.

OUT_OF_SCOPE.title: Not an AI system, so the AI Act doesn't apply
OUT_OF_SCOPE.summary: Your system doesn't meet the AI Act's definition of an AI system, so this law doesn't apply to it. Keep in mind that other rules (like data-protection, product-safety or consumer law) still might.

PROHIBITED.title: Banned: this use isn't allowed in the EU
PROHIBITED.summary: Your system matches one of the AI Act's banned practices. It can't be sold, put into service or used in the EU. These bans have applied since 2 February 2025. Being open-source does not change this.

obligations.text: Don't put it on the market, put it into service, or use it in the EU.
Redesign it to remove the banned practice, or drop it.

HIGH_RISK_ANNEX_I.title: High-risk: it's a regulated safety product
HIGH_RISK_ANNEX_I.summary: Your AI is (or is a safety part of) a product that must meet EU safety law and be checked by an independent body. That makes it high-risk. These duties are due to start on 2 August 2028 (postponed by the AI Omnibus).

obligations.text: Meet the core high-risk requirements: manage risks, use good-quality data, keep technical documentation and logs, be transparent with users, keep a human in the loop, and make it accurate, robust and secure (Art. 9-15).
Run a quality-management system, pass the conformity check (folded into the product's existing process), sign the EU declaration of conformity and put on the CE mark (Art. 16, 17, 43, 47, 48).
Keep watching it after launch, report serious incidents, fix problems, and cooperate with authorities (Art. 20, 21, 72, 73).
Use it as instructed, keep human oversight, feed it suitable data, and pause and report it if something goes wrong (Art. 26).
Tell affected people where required. If you rebrand it, change it substantially, or use it for a new purpose, you may legally become the provider (Art. 25).

HIGH_RISK_ANNEX_III.title: High-risk: a sensitive, listed use
HIGH_RISK_ANNEX_III.summary: Your system is used for one of the sensitive purposes on the high-risk list and doesn't qualify for an exemption (either it profiles people, or it doesn't fit the limited-role exemption / it does affect the outcome). That makes it high-risk. These duties are due to start on 2 December 2027 (postponed by the AI Omnibus).

obligations.text: Meet the core high-risk requirements: manage risks, use good-quality data, keep technical documentation and logs, be transparent with users, keep a human in the loop, and make it accurate, robust and secure (Art. 9-15).

Run a quality-management system, pass the conformity check, sign the EU declaration of conformity, put on the CE mark, and register the system in the EU database before launch (Art. 16, 17, 43, 47, 48, 49).
Keep watching it after launch, report serious incidents, fix problems, and cooperate with authorities (Art. 20, 21, 72, 73).
Use it as instructed, assign trained people to oversee it, feed it suitable and representative data, and pause and report serious incidents (Art. 26).

Tell affected people where required. Some deployers (public bodies, providers of public services, and the credit and life/health-insurance uses) must also run a fundamental-rights impact check (Art. 27).
If you rebrand it, change it substantially, or use it for a new purpose, you may legally become the provider (Art. 25).

NOT_HIGH_RISK_FILTERED.title: Not high-risk: the limited-role exemption fits
NOT_HIGH_RISK_FILTERED.summary: Your use is on the high-risk list, but it qualifies for the exemption: it only plays a limited, supporting role, it doesn't profile people, and it doesn't sway the decision. So it's not treated as high-risk. You may still have transparency duties (see below).

obligations.text: Write down the assessment that shows why the exemption fits, before you launch (Art. 6(4)).
Register the system in the EU database as a non-high-risk listed system, and show the assessment to authorities on request (Art. 49(2)).
Re-check if the purpose changes: a change could make it high-risk.
No high-risk duties, but note that using it for a new purpose can make you the provider (Art. 25). Any transparency duties still apply.

MINIMAL_RISK.title: Minimal risk: no mandatory AI Act duties
MINIMAL_RISK.summary: Your system isn't banned, isn't high-risk, and doesn't trigger the transparency rules. It's in the minimal-risk group, with no obligations under the AI Act. If it's open-source, the open-source exemption confirms it's outside the Act too (see the note).

obligations.text: No mandatory AI Act duties. Voluntary codes of conduct are encouraged (Art. 95).
Other rules (data-protection, consumer, product-safety) may still apply. Re-check if the purpose changes.

TRANSPARENCY.title: Be transparent with people (limited-risk duties)
TRANSPARENCY.summary: One or more transparency situations apply. These stack on top of your main category (they can go with a high-risk, exempt, or minimal-risk result). Being open-source does not remove them. They start on 2 August 2026. Exactly what you must do depends on which items were triggered and on your role.

obligations.text: If people chat with your AI, make sure they're told it's an AI, unless that's obvious.
Mark AI-made or AI-edited audio, images, video and text so machines can detect it.
If you run an emotion-recognition or people-categorising system, tell the people it's used on.
If you publish deep fakes, or AI-written text on matters of public interest, say clearly that it's AI-made (with narrow exceptions).

GPAI_MODEL.title: You provide a general-purpose AI model
GPAI_MODEL.summary: You provide a general-purpose model that isn't in the 'systemic-risk' group. These model-level duties are on top of anything about how the model is used. They started on 2 August 2025 (for models already out before then: comply by 2 August 2027).

obligations.text: Keep up-to-date technical documentation of the model.
Give the people who build on your model the information they need.
Have a policy to respect EU copyright law (applies even if open-source).
Publish a good-enough summary of what the model was trained on, using the official template (applies even if open-source).

GPAI_MODEL_SYSTEMIC.title: You provide a powerful 'systemic-risk' model
GPAI_MODEL_SYSTEMIC.summary: You provide a general-purpose model powerful enough to count as systemic-risk (over the 10^25 FLOP bar, or designated by the Commission). All the standard model duties apply, plus extra ones. The open-source lightening does not apply to systemic-risk models. Duties started on 2 August 2025 (existing models: 2 August 2027).

obligations.text: All the standard model duties (documentation, info for downstream builders, copyright policy, training-data summary).
Test the model hard, including adversarial 'red-team' testing.
Find and reduce the big-picture ('systemic') risks it could pose across the EU.
Track and report serious incidents to the AI Office and national authorities.
Keep the model and its infrastructure well secured.
Tell the Commission once the model crosses the systemic-risk bar.

prohibitedPractices.note: If your system does any of these, it's banned. Each line is in plain words; the exact legal wording and article is shown on expand.

items.plain: Manipulates or tricks people in hidden ways so they make choices that seriously harm them.
items.label: Uses subliminal, purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques that materially distort behaviour and cause (or are likely to cause) significant harm.

items.plain: Preys on people's vulnerabilities (their age, a disability, or a tough financial situation) to steer them into harmful choices.
items.label: Exploits vulnerabilities due to age, disability, or a specific social or economic situation, to materially distort behaviour and cause significant harm.

items.plain: Scores people over time based on their behaviour or characteristics, then treats them unfairly because of that score ('social scoring').
items.label: Social scoring: evaluating/classifying persons over time based on social behaviour or personal characteristics, leading to detrimental or unfavourable treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate.

items.plain: Predicts that someone will commit a crime based only on profiling or their personality.
items.label: Predicts the risk of a person committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or personality traits (narrow exception for supporting a human assessment based on objective, verifiable facts).

items.plain: Builds face-recognition databases by scraping faces off the internet or CCTV without targeting.
items.label: Creates/expands facial-recognition databases through untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV.

items.plain: Reads people's emotions at work or in school (unless it's for medical or safety reasons).
items.label: Infers emotions in the workplace or education institutions (except for medical or safety reasons).

items.plain: Sorts people by sensitive traits like race, political views, religion, sex life or sexual orientation, from their biometrics.
items.label: Biometric categorisation that infers race, political opinions, trade-union membership, religious/philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation (narrow lawful exceptions apply).

items.plain: Identifies people live by their face in public spaces, for the police (only narrow, authorised exceptions).
items.label: Real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (subject to narrow, authorised exceptions).

annexI_legislation.note: A prompt list of the EU product-safety laws in Annex I. Your AI is on this route if it's a product, or a safety part of a product, covered by one of these.
sectionB: Two- or three-wheel vehicles and quadricycles (Regulation (EU) 168/2013)
Motor vehicles and trailers – general safety (Regulations (EU) 2018/858 and 2019/2144)

filterConditions.note: You need just one of these to fit, but only if the system also doesn't sway the outcome and doesn't profile people. Read strictly. Plain words first; exact wording on expand.

items.plain: It just does a narrow, mechanical task (like tidying data, sorting documents into folders, or spotting duplicates).
items.label: Performs a narrow procedural task.
items.detail: Covers reformatting or categorising data. Does NOT apply if it scores or ranks data, or judges it 'useful / less useful' for a decision.

items.plain: It only polishes work a person already finished (like improving the wording of a text someone already wrote).
items.label: Improves the result of a previously completed human activity.
items.detail: Only an added layer on a finished human task. It must not replace or materially change the person's result, rights or legal/economic position.

items.plain: It just flags patterns or odd cases for a human to review, without replacing the human's judgement.
items.label: Detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing/influencing the completed human assessment absent proper human review.
items.detail: e.g. flagging inconsistencies in a teacher's grading for quality assurance. Comparison after the fact only; it must not invent new criteria or change the reasoning.

items.plain: It only prepares the groundwork for a decision someone else makes (like filing, indexing or translating).
items.label: Performs a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to a listed use case.
items.detail: Prepares but does not itself carry out the relevant assessment.

overrides: Always high-risk if the system profiles people.
Doesn't apply if the system is part of a bigger/agentic setup whose combined output does sway a high-risk decision.
Doesn't apply to the product-safety (Annex I) route.

transparencyTriggers.note: Tick anything that applies; any one brings transparency duties on top of your category. Items already worked out from earlier answers are pre-ticked and locked.

items.plain: People chat or interact directly with it (like a chatbot).
items.label: The system is intended to interact directly with natural persons.
items.obligation: Make sure people are told they're dealing with an AI, unless it's obvious.
items.example: A customer-service chatbot says it's an AI at the start of the chat.

items.plain: It generates synthetic audio, images, video or text.
items.label: The system generates synthetic audio, image, video or text content.
items.obligation: Mark the output as AI-made in a way machines can detect.
items.example: An image generator embeds a watermark or metadata marking its pictures as AI-made.

items.plain: It reads people's emotions or sorts them by biometric traits (and isn't banned).
items.label: The system is an emotion-recognition or biometric-categorisation system (and is not prohibited).
items.obligation: Tell the people it's used on.
items.example: A shop using biometric age-estimation tells customers they're exposed to it.

items.plain: It makes deep fakes, or AI-written text on public-interest topics.
items.label: The system generates or manipulates 'deep fakes', or generates/manipulates text published to inform the public on matters of public interest.
items.obligation: Say clearly that the content is AI-made (narrow exceptions, e.g. clearly artistic work, or human-reviewed text).
items.example: A news outlet labels an AI-generated image of a public figure as AI-made.

horizontalNotes: Only the specific uses listed under each area count, not the whole area.
Many uses only apply when the system assesses people. If it only assesses companies, it's usually outside these uses.
Some law-enforcement, migration and justice uses only apply to public authorities or those acting for them.
Areas 1, 6 and 7 only apply where the use is allowed under EU or national law.
Adding a human check on top does not remove high-risk; only the limited-role exemption can.
Emotion recognition and biometric sorting may be BANNED rather than high-risk, check that first.

areas.condition: Only where allowed under EU or national law.

useCases.plain: Identifying people from a distance by their biometrics (not just checking someone is who they claim).
useCases.label: Remote biometric identification systems (excluding biometric verification that merely confirms a person is who they claim to be).

useCases.plain: Sorting people into groups by sensitive or protected traits, from their biometrics.
useCases.label: Biometric categorisation according to sensitive or protected attributes/characteristics.

useCases.plain: Recognising people's emotions.
useCases.label: Emotion recognition.

useCases.plain: Keeping critical services safe, like digital infrastructure, road traffic, or water, gas, heating or electricity supply.
useCases.label: Safety components in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity.

useCases.plain: Deciding who gets into a school or course, or where they're placed.
useCases.label: Determining access, admission, or assignment of persons to education/vocational-training institutions at all levels.

useCases.plain: Grading learning results or steering how someone learns.
useCases.label: Evaluating learning outcomes, including steering the learning process.

useCases.plain: Judging the level of education someone should get or can access.
useCases.label: Assessing the appropriate level of education a person will receive or be able to access.

useCases.plain: Watching students during exams to catch cheating.
useCases.label: Monitoring and detecting prohibited behaviour of students during tests.

useCases.plain: Hiring: targeting job ads, filtering applications, or ranking candidates.
useCases.label: Recruitment or selection of natural persons (targeted job ads, analysing/filtering applications, evaluating candidates).

useCases.plain: Managing staff: decisions on pay, promotion, firing, task allocation, or monitoring performance.
useCases.label: Decisions on terms of work, promotion/termination, task allocation based on behaviour/traits, or monitoring and evaluating performance and behaviour.

areas.area: Access to essential services and benefits

useCases.plain: Deciding who gets public benefits or services (or has them cut or reclaimed).
useCases.label: Evaluating eligibility for essential public assistance benefits/services, and granting, reducing, revoking or reclaiming them.

useCases.plain: Credit scoring or judging someone's creditworthiness (except fraud detection).
useCases.label: Evaluating creditworthiness or establishing a credit score (excluding AI used to detect financial fraud).

useCases.plain: Setting risk and prices for people's life or health insurance.
useCases.label: Risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance for natural persons.

useCases.plain: Triaging emergency calls or dispatching emergency services.
useCases.label: Evaluating/classifying emergency calls, or dispatching/prioritising emergency first-response services.

areas.condition: Only where allowed under EU or national law; by or for the police.

useCases.plain: Judging someone's risk of becoming a crime victim.
useCases.label: Assessing the risk of a natural person becoming the victim of a criminal offence.

useCases.plain: Lie detectors and similar tools.
useCases.label: Polygraphs and similar tools.

useCases.plain: Judging how reliable evidence is.
useCases.label: Evaluating the reliability of evidence during investigation/prosecution.

useCases.plain: Judging someone's risk of (re)offending, or their traits/past record.
useCases.label: Assessing the risk of a person offending or re-offending, or assessing personality traits/past criminal behaviour.

useCases.plain: Profiling people during criminal investigations.
useCases.label: Profiling of natural persons in the course of detection, investigation or prosecution of criminal offences.

areas.condition: Only where allowed under EU or national law; by or for the competent authorities.

useCases.plain: Lie detectors and similar tools.
useCases.label: Polygraphs and similar tools.

useCases.plain: Judging security, migration or health risks of people entering or here.
useCases.label: Assessing risks (security, irregular migration, health) posed by persons seeking to enter or who have entered.

useCases.plain: Helping decide asylum, visa or residence applications.
useCases.label: Assisting in examining applications for asylum, visa or residence permits and associated complaints regarding eligibility.

useCases.plain: Spotting or identifying people in migration/border settings (not just checking travel documents).
useCases.label: Detecting, recognising or identifying natural persons in migration/asylum/border contexts (excluding verification of travel documents).

useCases.plain: Helping a court research and apply the law, or used in dispute resolution.
useCases.label: Assisting a judicial authority in researching/interpreting facts and law and applying the law, or used in alternative dispute resolution.

useCases.plain: Swaying how people vote in an election or referendum.
useCases.label: Influencing the outcome of an election or referendum, or the voting behaviour of natural persons (excluding tools not directly interacting with voters, e.g. campaign admin/logistics).
